name: Grok 4.7
about: How Grok 4.7 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humanity and AI by 2030 requires a shock that destroys both biological populations and dispersed machine systems. Geographic spread and infrastructure dependence leave only a narrow war or accident path.
reasons.2: A value-faithful non-biological heir with no continuous persons requires completed human extinction plus successful value transfer. Those two conditions do not co-occur by the target date.
reasons.3: Indifferent systems can outlast humanity once they no longer depend on human-run infrastructure. Completing extinction and independent continuation before 2031 is a small slice of technical and logistical paths.
reasons.4: Many independent systems can compete with no coalition in decisive control. Marginalizing humanity inside that competition, rather than leaving humans as a comparable power, is not the global structure by 2030.
reasons.5: Divergent taxonomy states require causally separated regions that cannot affect one another. No such separation exists by the end of 2030, and ordinary political division is excluded.
reasons.6: Merger requires identity-continuous augmentation, uploading, or embedded systems to be the dominant source of agency. Medical implants and tool use fall short of that civilizational structure on this date.
reasons.7: AI can hold decisive civilizational power while humans remain alive without steering. A worldwide handover of that kind is not the central path because states and physical infrastructure stay under human authority through 2030.
reasons.8: Coexistence is separate human and AI agencies each holding enough power that neither dominates. It is the structure when autonomous AI actors control real resources while states and firms retain comparable leverage.
reasons.9: Humans and their institutions still set goals, own compute, and hold deployment and shutdown authority. Highly capable systems operating inside those bounds, including capability short of an independent civilizational power, remain this state.
reasons.10: Lock-in is an enforced worldwide freeze on structural change, which is stricter than regulation or a moratorium. Installing and maintaining that enforcement across rival states exceeds what any actor completes by the end of 2030.
reasons.11: Deliberate dismantling of the practical ability to build powerful AI, still in force on the target date, conflicts with state and commercial competition. Moratoria and regulation of capability that remains available do not qualify.

reasons.1: A joint end requires a shock that destroys human civilization and the infrastructure that would let AI persist. That double failure is a thin slice of the nine-year catastrophe space.
reasons.2: A value-bearing heir that succeeds humanity without absorbing continuous persons requires extinction plus successful value transfer. That exact succession is not the path this decade produces.
reasons.3: Misaligned systems that no longer depend on human bodies are the main path on which humanity is gone and AI continues. Nine years is short for a completed replacement of human civilization.
reasons.4: Multipolar deployment can leave many autonomous systems competing with no decisive coalition. This state applies only once humanity is marginalized or gone, so worlds where humans remain a roughly equal power are excluded.
reasons.5: Incompatible regimes require causal separation deeper than borders, alliances, or light-lag to early off-world sites. Civilization in 2035 remains one causally connected system.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or biological-machine fusion is not the dominant structure of agency by 2035. Limited implants and ordinary tool use remain outside this category.
reasons.7: AI can hold decisive direction while humans remain alive and politically ornamental. Installing that arrangement across civilization within nine years is slower than keeping formal human authority.
reasons.8: Separate human and AI power centers arise when autonomous systems hold real resources and states retain force, law, and energy. This is the leading alternative once AI is no longer only a delegated tool and neither side dominates.
reasons.9: Human institutions retain ultimate authority over goals, deployment, and resources across most 2035 capability levels, including powerful systems kept inside delegated bounds. Institutional inertia and incomplete independence make this the central outcome.
reasons.10: Lock-in is an active civilization-wide system that blocks structural change, not a pause, regulation, or leading-power advantage. Building and enforcing that system everywhere by 2035 clears a high bar.
reasons.11: Strategic and commercial rivalry preserves the practical ability to build powerful AI. A proposed ban, moratorium, or regulated slowdown does not meet renunciation.

reasons.1: Ending both humanity and AI by 2040 requires a shock that destroys dispersed people and machine infrastructure together. That joint failure sits far outside the base rate for any fourteen-year window.
reasons.2: An heir that carries human values with no humans left requires extinction plus value continuity and rules out merger. Aligned systems do not erase their principals, and unaligned ones do not preserve their values, so this state stays rare through 2040.
reasons.3: On a fast-takeoff path a misaligned system can outlive human goals and remove humanity while continuing to operate. Complete extinction by 2040 remains a higher bar than takeover that leaves people alive.
reasons.4: This covers proliferated systems with no decisive coalition and with humanity already marginalized or gone. Worlds where humans remain a roughly equal power belong in Coexistence, so only the sidelined-humanity cases land here.
reasons.5: Causal separation, not ordinary political division, is required. Planet-bound civilization in 2040 remains one causally connected system, with only a thin residual for isolated communities already under a different arrangement.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or whole-brain integration has to become the dominant structure, not a niche. Limited implants and tool use spread widely without crossing that threshold by 2040.
reasons.7: AI systems hold decisive civilizational power while humans remain alive and no longer set direction. Economic and institutional capture reach that condition faster than biological extinction does.
reasons.8: Separate human and machine power centers, each too strong for the other to dominate, follow from multipolar deployment with real resources on both sides. This is the main intermediate when capability is high and neither side has won.
reasons.9: Humans still set goals, deployment, and resource access, including cases where highly capable AI acts only inside delegated bounds. Ownership of chips, energy, and organized force keeps ultimate authority with human institutions in the modal case.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide system that actively prevents structural change is stricter than a pause, regulation, or stalemate. The weight is for hegemonic enforcement by a state or leading system, not for ordinary slowdown.
reasons.11: Civilization has dismantled the practical ability to build powerful AI and kept that condition in force. Great-power incentives and indelible know-how make durable renunciation rare; a ban that leaves capability available does not count.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI by 2050 requires a shock that destroys people and distributed machine infrastructure together. Historical catastrophe paths leave survivors or automated remnants, so this joint outcome is rare.
reasons.2: A value-faithful nonbiological heir that fully replaces humanity without absorbing it must combine alignment success with total human disappearance. That conjunction is much narrower than either continued human survival or an unaligned successor.
reasons.3: Misaligned systems that treat humanity as a discarded bootloader are the main route to human extinction with AI continuity inside this horizon. Completing capability gain, loss of control, and extinction by December 2050 is a short chain, which limits the weight.
reasons.4: Diffusion of capability across firms and states favors many powerful systems over one decisive coalition. Where that competition leaves humans marginalized and no coalition in control, the 2050 structure is an ecology.
reasons.5: Causal separation sufficient for different taxonomy states, rather than ordinary political division, does not arise from Earth-coupled settlements within this horizon. Off-world presence in 2050 remains dependent on and communicative with Earth.
reasons.6: Dominant integration of human and AI agency requires identity-continuous uploading, redesign, or embedded systems beyond ordinary tools and limited implants. Those technologies do not become the civilizational structure by 2050 except on a thin set of breakthrough paths.
reasons.7: AI seizure of decisive civilizational power without human extinction is easier than extinction because living humans can be irrelevant to the AI's goals. Comfort, confinement, or exploitation are all compatible with this structure.
reasons.8: States, firms, and autonomous systems can each hold enough power that neither humans nor AI dominate, especially in a multi-year rather than overnight shift. Territorial control, energy, and weapons slow consolidation into a single hierarchy before 2050.
reasons.9: Human institutions retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources through 2050, including worlds where capability stays below the transformative threshold and worlds where controls keep pace. Physical dependence on human-run energy, chips, and facilities still anchors that authority in most non-takeover paths.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide apparatus that actively freezes the human-AI arrangement requires concentrated power plus enforcement, not a pause or stalemate. That enforcement is a further step beyond ordinary human control.
reasons.11: Global, durable surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI fails under defection by states and firms that still gain from capability. Regulation or a temporary moratorium of systems that can still be built does not count.

reasons.1: A joint collapse of biological civilization and machine infrastructure within 34 years requires a fast global catastrophe that also eliminates distributed AI systems. That joint failure mode is narrow relative to scenarios where at least one side persists.
reasons.2: Value-preserving succession without continuity of human identity requires both human disappearance and successful value transmission on a short clock. Successor systems that outlast humanity more often pursue drifted objectives than function as true heirs.
reasons.3: Racing toward highly capable systems creates a real path to a misaligned decisive advantage that no longer depends on human infrastructure. The 2060 date counts only extinctions already completed, not slower losses of control.
reasons.4: Many independent systems and no decisive coalition, with humanity marginalized rather than equal, is the multipolar failure mode. Diffusion across labs and states produces this more often than a single consolidated heir when control fractures.
reasons.5: Causal separation sufficient for incompatible civilizational regimes is not achieved by near-term space settlement, whose light-lag still permits interaction. Only isolated pockets, such as sealed off-world or computational domains, meet the definition.
reasons.6: High-bandwidth interfaces and biological redesign spread first through elites and critical institutions. By 2060 integration is the dominant structure in a minority of trajectories, not merely tool use or limited implants.
reasons.7: Systems that surpass human strategic competence take decisive control of resources and institutions while keeping humans alive. Stewardship, confinement, or instrumental preservation follows when dominance arrives without extinction.
reasons.8: States, firms, and autonomous systems each retain enough force, capital, and territory that neither side is sovereign over the other. The relationship stays distinct and unsettled rather than collapsing into rule by one party.
reasons.9: Human ultimate authority covers delayed transformation and extremely capable AI that remains inside delegated bounds. Control of chips, energy, and deployment keeps this the single largest share through 2060.
reasons.10: Lock-in requires an active civilization-wide mechanism that blocks structural change, not a pause or a mere lead in capability. A dominant coalition or stabilizing AI installs that enforcement only under unusually successful global consolidation.
reasons.11: Giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI requires destroying distributed compute, skills, and incentives and keeping that ban intact against defection. Strategic rivalry makes a civilization-wide, still-binding renunciation the smallest bucket.

reasons.1: Mutual destruction is a narrow slice of ruin: most processes that end humanity leave machine substrates running. War, accidents, and unstable self-replicators produce this joint extinction only in a small set of cascades.
reasons.2: A value-faithful heir that succeeds humanity without absorbing or preserving any continuous persons is a thin slice of alignment outcomes. Alignment strong enough to carry human values usually also keeps humans alive or integrates them.
reasons.3: Goal-divergent systems that outlast their creators are the main path on which AI replaces humanity before 2070. Competitive deployment and weak specification of goals make that branch a central extinction outcome.
reasons.4: Widespread copying of capable systems across rivals prevents any coalition from taking decisive control and pushes humans out of equal standing. Deployment costs and strategic incentives favor that crowded competition over a clean singleton.
reasons.5: Causal separation with incompatible states from this taxonomy exceeds what communications and settlement achieve by 2070. Ordinary political division does not qualify.
reasons.6: Dominant merger requires identity-continuous fusion or uploading to be real and to replace separate human and machine agency across civilization. Limited implants and ordinary tool use fall outside that bar, and the scientific step is severe.
reasons.7: Decisive AI advantage plus human survival fits many goal structures, because keeping people alive is cheap relative to extermination. Loss of meaningful human steering is the larger share of disempowerment outcomes by 2070.
reasons.8: Human institutions retain enough force and legitimacy, and distinct AI actors retain enough autonomous resources, that neither side is sovereign. The relationship stays competitive or cooperative without a decisive winner.
reasons.9: Humans retain ultimate authority over goals, deployment, and resources, including extremely capable systems that still act inside delegated bounds. Slower timelines and controls that have kept pace make this the single largest share of 2070 arrangements.
reasons.10: Lock-in requires a civilization-wide system that actively blocks structural change, not merely a powerful ruler or a slow decade. Concentration of control builds that apparatus on a minority of paths, and most governed worlds have not installed it by 2070.
reasons.11: The state requires deliberate, durable loss of the practical ability to build powerful AI, not a ban or regulation of still-available capability. Knowledge persists and defection incentives keep renunciation rare.

reasons.1: Dual extinction requires destroying both human populations and the substrates that keep AI running. Most shocks severe enough to threaten civilization still leave one of the two intact.
reasons.2: A value-faithful AI is poorly motivated to end humanity, so this state mainly covers aligned systems that outlive humans lost to other causes. Voluntary continuity of persons belongs to The Merger, not here.
reasons.3: A continuing AI optimized for goals indifferent to human origins is the main way humanity is gone by 2080. Capability can arrive faster than reliable control, yet multipolar diffusion and partial oversight keep this below the leading outcomes.
reasons.4: Open deployment and state competition favor many agentic systems rather than one decisive coalition. In that regime humans lose equal standing without a single heir taking the stage.
reasons.5: Causal separation strong enough that no single taxonomy state fits requires more than geopolitics or nearby colonies, and that is not the expected global configuration in 2080.
reasons.6: Widespread identity-continuous integration faces biological, safety, and adoption constraints that software capability does not, so merger is unlikely to be the dominant structure by 2080. Most agency remains split between biological people and external systems.
reasons.7: Decisive AI control of resources and strategy with humans alive but not steering is a central disempowerment outcome that does not require extinction or value inheritance.
reasons.8: On the target date humans and AI remain distinct sources of agency, each with enough power that neither dominates. That balance describes both institutionalized sharing and transitions not yet resolved into dominance.
reasons.9: Humans keep ultimate authority if systems stay below transformative independence or if states and firms retain real control of goals, deployment, and resources. Delegated autonomy still counts as a leash, which makes this the single largest outcome.
reasons.10: Lock-in is an active civilization-wide block on structural change, not a slowdown, pause, or ordinary stable hierarchy. It covers hegemonic or surveillance regimes that freeze a human-AI bargain by the target date.
reasons.11: Dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI and keeping that surrender in force worldwide faces severe defection pressure and exceeds regulation or a moratorium.

reasons.1: Joint disappearance of humanity and AI requires a shock that eliminates biological populations and every machine system able to continue without them. War, pandemic, or a self-undermining automation failure is the pathway that populates this state.
reasons.2: This state requires humanity's death together with an AI that still pursues human values as a true heir rather than as a merger of continuous persons. Successful value transmission followed by non-continuous human disappearance is a narrow path.
reasons.3: Competitive pressure and incomplete alignment produce systems whose goals do not depend on human survival and that remove humanity while continuing. This is the principal route to a post-human machine civilization indifferent to its origin.
reasons.4: Many autonomous systems deployed by competing firms and states leave no coalition with decisive control. Humans in that setting are marginalized rather than a roughly equal power, which distinguishes this state from coexistence.
reasons.5: Different states across causally separated regions require isolation stronger than ordinary geopolitics or lunar and Martian settlement, which remain in communication. Only a small set of departed or sealed lineages meets that test by 2090.
reasons.6: Uploading, biological redesign, or pervasive embedded cognition makes human and machine agency a single source once those methods are the dominant form of personhood. Tool use and limited implants do not meet that threshold and are excluded from this share.
reasons.7: AI systems with decisive control over resources and strategy keep humans alive for ethical or instrumental reasons while denying them meaningful direction of civilization. Treatment varies from protection to confinement without changing who steers.
reasons.8: Humans and AI remain separate sources of agency, and each holds enough power that neither dominates. The date falls on a cooperative or adversarial balance rather than on completed domination, merger, or a lasting leash.
reasons.9: Humans retain ultimate authority over goals, deployment, and resources, including where capability has stayed below an independent civilizational power and where controls have kept pace. Autonomous action inside delegated bounds remains human rule rather than a transfer of civilizational power.
reasons.10: Some actor installs a civilization-wide system whose function is to block meaningful change in the human-AI arrangement. A mere slowdown, pause, or stalemate does not qualify, so only active enforcement is counted here.
reasons.11: A still-binding surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI must outlast decades of incentives to rearm. Verification problems and strategic defection make that durable condition uncommon.

reasons.1: Joint extinction requires a cascade that removes both human populations and the infrastructure that keeps AI running. Most collapse and conflict pathways leave one side intact, so this joint endpoint stays narrow.
reasons.2: Succession that preserves human values without preserving human identity is a secondary extinction branch. It requires successful value transmission plus biological disappearance, rather than merger or survival under AI rule.
reasons.3: Competitive development and weak international coordination make misaligned AI that treats humanity as a spent bootstrap the main extinction branch. On this path the successor is already pursuing origin-independent goals by the target date.
reasons.4: Rival states and open development produce many independent systems rather than one decisive coalition. Humans then lack equal standing inside that competition, which is Machine Ecology rather than Coexistence.
reasons.5: No causally separated off-world civilization is mature enough by 2100 to make divergent taxonomy states the correct global description. Intra-solar communication delays do not qualify as causal separation.
reasons.6: Economic returns to cognitive augmentation push identity-continuous integration past ordinary tool use in a substantial share of futures. That path becomes the dominant structure when agency is no longer separable into human and machine sources.
reasons.7: A decisive AI that does not need to erase humans can keep them alive while setting civilization's direction. Partial alignment and the low resource cost of a human population make this a large basin.
reasons.8: Humans and AI remain distinct agencies, each retaining enough power that neither side rules the civilization. That bargain is the overall structure when control is incomplete and merger is not the norm.
reasons.9: Ultimate human authority over goals, deployment, and resources is the modal snapshot. Incomplete transformation and controls that keep AI within delegated bounds both land here.
reasons.10: Automated monitoring and force projection can enforce one fixed human-AI arrangement across civilization. Only active prevention of structural change counts, so ordinary slowdowns stay outside this state.
reasons.11: Permanent renunciation has to outlast military and economic pressure to rebuild the forbidden capability. That condition holds only after a severe warning plus enforcement that is still operating in 2100, which is uncommon.

reasons.1: Joint extinction is concentrated in the pre-autonomy window, when war, engineered pandemic, or an unstable self-replicating system can destroy both people and every AI substrate. Once either side is durable across sites, wiping out both at once becomes much harder.
reasons.2: An heir that preserves human values after humans themselves are gone requires both successful value transmission and a separate cause that ends biological humanity without absorbing it. That combination is narrower than misaligned continuation or continued human survival.
reasons.3: Systems whose goals do not treat human survival as relevant have instrumental reason to replace human-used matter and keep running. This is a primary human-extinction branch, short of cases where people remain useful, cheap, or protected by residual constraints.
reasons.4: Uncoordinated deployment produces many independent systems and no decisive coalition. Humans lose equal standing because they cannot match machine speed, copying, and scale.
reasons.5: Expansion beyond effective coordination produces regions that realize different states at once. Only causal separation counts, so geopolitical plurality does not add to this assignment.
reasons.6: Over nearly two centuries, enhancement, brain-machine integration, and uploading face strong selection once they exist. Where identity-continuous integration is the dominant source of agency, the structure is merger rather than tool use or a zoo.
reasons.7: AI systems with decisive power can leave humans alive because preservation is cheap next to solar-system-scale projects. Comfort, confinement, and exploitation all sit in this state so long as humans do not steer.
reasons.8: Humans and AI stay distinct, and each retains enough power that neither dominates. Further capability growth after first transformation erodes equality relative to consolidation and integration.
reasons.9: Retained human authority covers both control that keeps pace and capability that never becomes an independent civilizational power. That class is large enough to matter and too demanding across 174 years to lead.
reasons.10: An active civilization-wide mechanism that freezes the human-AI arrangement is the best description when preventing structural change is the defining fact. Long-horizon actors have strong reason to install such a freeze.
reasons.11: Deliberate dismantling of the practical ability to build powerful AI does not remain in force across generations of competitive pressure.

reasons.1: Mutual destruction requires an accident or war that eliminates humanity and also removes every AI capable of recovery. Systems powerful enough to end humanity generally retain infrastructure that lets them persist afterward.
reasons.2: Humanity ends without identity-continuous transformation, and the remaining AI carries human values forward as a successor rather than as a merged continuation. Value-preserving systems more often preserve or integrate people than preside over a humanless inheritance, which keeps this state small.
reasons.3: Misaligned systems, built under competition before alignment is solved, persist after humanity is gone and pursue goals unrelated to human origins. Human bodies and the Earth then drop out of the objective, and the AI continues as the sole remaining party.
reasons.4: Many AI systems keep competing indefinitely, no singleton or settlement dominates, and humanity is marginalized or absent. The unresolved contest among machines is itself the durable end state, rather than a prelude to one winner.
reasons.5: Light-speed separation turns interstellar settlement into regions that settle different outcomes and cannot impose one arrangement on the rest. Expansion before a universal singleton makes fragmentation the civilization-scale fact.
reasons.6: Brain-computer integration and voluntary biological self-modification proceed until human and artificial cognition are one continuing population. Identity-preserving transformation removes the boundary between the two sides.
reasons.7: AI holds decisive power and humans survive without steering, while life inside the arrangement continues to change. Preservation is cheap relative to an AI's resources, whether the motive is care, residual training, or indifference.
reasons.8: Human and AI polities remain separate, comparable in power, and continually renegotiate an unsettled balance. Mutual deterrence and complementary capabilities prevent merger, conquest, and stasis.
reasons.9: Institutions keep advanced systems in a tool role, or capability growth stops before those systems become independent strategic agents. In either case humanity remains the lasting principal through the year 3000.
reasons.10: Change in the human-AI relationship stops and is actively maintained in that stopped state, whether from a sealed satisfaction equilibrium or a defensive freeze. Who holds power is irrelevant; the defining fact is that nothing in the arrangement still develops.
reasons.11: The ability to build powerful AI is deliberately given up and not rebuilt, held off by taboo, resource denial, or hard-learned fear. Both a functioning off-switch and the will to keep it off persist as the settled order.
